title: Probability and Statistics for AI
summary: Machine learning is fundamentally about reasoning under uncertainty. Statistics helps you understand your data's distribution, spot patterns, and quantify confidence. Probability underpins models like Naive Bayes and concepts like likelihood. Knowing
content:
# Probability and Statistics for AI ##### The 95%-accurate test that is wrong most of the time A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test detects it correctly 99% of the time and produces a false positive only 5% of the time. You test positive. Most people — including most doctors, in repeated studies — estimate the probability you have the disease at around 95%. The actual answer is roughly **2%**. Work through 100,000 people. About 100 have the disease, and the test correctly flags 99 of them. The other 99,900 are healthy, and 5% of those — 4,995 people — test positive anyway. So 5,094 positive results, of which 99 are real: **1.9%**. The intuition fails because it ignores the **base rate**. The disease is so rare that false positives from the huge healthy population overwhelm true positives from the tiny sick one. This matters directly for machine learning. Fraud detection, disease screening, defect identification and churn prediction all involve rare positive classes, and a model reporting 99% accuracy on a 1%-positive dataset may simply be predicting "no" every time. Statistics is what stops you being fooled by your own metrics. ##### Probability fundamentals Probability quantifies uncertainty on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). - **Joint probability** `P(A and B)` — both occur. - **Conditional probability** `P(A | B)` — A occurs *given that* B occurred. - **Independence** — knowing B tells you nothing about A, so `P(A|B) = P(A)`. The conditional definition is the one to remember: ```text P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B) ``` Conditional probability *is* prediction. A classifier estimating whether a customer will churn is computing `P(churn | age, tenure, spend, tickets)` — the probability of an outcome given evidence. ##### Bayes' theorem Bayes' theorem (from Thomas Bayes' 1763 essay) lets you reverse a conditional — turning `P(evidence | hypothesis)`, which is often measurable, into `P(hypothesis | evidence)`, which is what you actually want: ```text P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B) ``` The named parts: `P(A)` is the **prior** (belief before evidence), `P(B|A)` is the **likelihood** (how probable the evidence is if A is true), and `P(A|B)` is the **posterior** (updated belief). ```python def bayes(prior: float, sensitivity: float, false_positive_rate: float) -> float: """P(disease | positive test).""" p_pos_given_disease = sensitivity p_pos_given_healthy = false_positive_rate p_positive = (p_pos_given_disease * prior + p_pos_given_healthy * (1 - prior)) return p_pos_given_disease * prior / p_positive print(f"{bayes(0.001, 0.99, 0.05):.3%}") # 1.943% # Test twice, independently — the second test starts from the updated prior after_one = bayes(0.001, 0.99, 0.05) print(f"{bayes(after_one, 0.99, 0.05):.1%}") # 28.2% ``` The second calculation shows Bayesian updating in action: evidence accumulates. One positive gives 2%, two independent positives give 28%. The practical lesson for ML: **a model's precision depends on the base rate, not only on its accuracy**. Deploy a fraud detector trained on a balanced dataset into production where fraud is 0.1% of transactions, and most of its alerts will be false alarms — even though nothing about the model changed. ##### Random variables and distributions A **random variable** maps outcomes to numbers. A **distribution** describes which values are likely. The **normal (Gaussian)** distribution — the bell curve — appears constantly because of the **Central Limit Theorem**: the average of many independent random effects tends toward normality regardless of the underlying distributions. Heights, measurement errors and model residuals are all approximately normal for this reason. ```python import numpy as np from scipy import stats rng = np.random.default_rng(42) heights = rng.normal(loc=165, scale=8, size=10_000) # mean 165cm, sd 8cm print(f"mean {heights.mean():.1f}, std {heights.std():.1f}") # The 68-95-99.7 rule within_1sd = np.mean(np.abs(heights - 165) < 8) within_2sd = np.mean(np.abs(heights - 165) < 16) print(f"within 1 sd: {within_1sd:.1%}, within 2 sd: {within_2sd:.1%}") # within 1 sd: 68.4%, within 2 sd: 95.5% ``` That **68-95-99.7 rule** is worth memorizing: roughly 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, 99.7% within three. It gives you an instant sense of whether a value is unusual, and it is the basis of the common "beyond 3 standard deviations" outlier rule. The **binomial** distribution models counts of successes in fixed trials: ```python # 100 emails, each 30% likely to be opened opens = rng.binomial(n=100, p=0.3, size=10_000) print(f"mean {opens.mean():.1f} (expected {100*0.3})") # Probability of 40 or more opens print(f"P(>=40) = {1 - stats.binom.cdf(39, 100, 0.3):.3%}") # 2.478% ``` Others you will meet: **Poisson** (events per interval — arrivals, defects), **uniform** (all values equally likely), and **exponential** (waiting times). ##### Mean, variance, standard deviation ```python data = np.array([12, 15, 11, 18, 95, 13, 14]) # note the outlier print(f"mean {np.mean(data):.2f}") # 25.43 — dragged by 95 print(f"median {np.median(data):.2f}") # 14.00 — unaffected print(f"std {np.std(data, ddof=1):.2f}") # 30.98 print(f"IQR {stats.iqr(data):.2f}") # 3.50 — robust spread ``` **The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is not.** One extreme value moved the mean from about 14 to 25. This is why you should look at both, and why median imputation is usually safer than mean imputation. **Variance** is the average squared deviation from the mean; **standard deviation** is its square root, expressed in the original units. Note `ddof=1` for a sample standard deviation — dividing by `n−1` rather than `n` corrects a bias when estimating from a sample. NumPy defaults to `ddof=0`, Pandas to `ddof=1`, which is a small inconsistency that occasionally surprises people. Standard deviation is what makes **standardization** work — `(x − mean) / std` converts any feature to mean 0, standard deviation 1, so features on wildly different scales become comparable. ##### Correlation is not causation **Correlation** measures how two variables move together, from −1 to +1: ```python x = rng.normal(0, 1, 500) y = 2 * x + rng.normal(0, 1, 500) pearson, p_value = stats.pearsonr(x, y) spearman, _ = stats.spearmanr(x, y) print(f"Pearson {pearson:.3f} (p={p_value:.2e})") # linear relationship print(f"Spearman {spearman:.3f}") # monotonic relationship ``` Use **Pearson** for linear relationships and **Spearman** when the relationship is monotonic but curved, or when outliers are present. Two cautions that matter operationally. **Correlation misses nonlinear relationships.** For `y = x²` with x centred on zero, Pearson correlation is approximately 0 despite a perfect deterministic relationship. Always plot; never rely on the coefficient alone. **Correlation does not imply causation.** Ice-cream sales correlate with drowning deaths; the cause is summer, a **confounding variable** affecting both. In ML this appears as leakage-like features: a model predicting hospital readmission might latch onto "number of prior appointments," which correlates with readmission but is a consequence of illness severity, not a cause of readmission. Such a feature can be predictive and still useless for intervention. ##### Hypothesis testing Hypothesis testing asks whether an observed difference is likely to be real or could plausibly be chance. The structure: a **null hypothesis** (no effect) and an **alternative** (an effect exists). You compute a **p-value** — the probability of seeing data at least this extreme *if the null were true* — and reject the null if it falls below a threshold, conventionally 0.05. ```python control = rng.normal(loc=0.10, scale=0.02, size=1000) # 10% conversion variant = rng.normal(loc=0.11, scale=0.02, size=1000) # 11% conversion t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(control, variant, equal_var=False) print(f"t = {t_stat:.3f}, p = {p_value:.2e}") # Effect size — how big is the difference, not just whether it exists pooled_sd = np.sqrt((control.std(ddof=1)**2 + variant.std(ddof=1)**2) / 2) cohens_d = (variant.mean() - control.mean()) / pooled_sd print(f"Cohen's d = {cohens_d:.3f}") ``` Three points that are widely misunderstood and worth stating plainly. **A p-value is not the probability the hypothesis is true.** It is the probability of the data given the null hypothesis — a different and much weaker statement. **Statistical significance is not practical importance.** With a large enough sample, a 0.01% difference becomes "significant." Always report the **effect size** alongside the p-value; Cohen's d around 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. **Testing many hypotheses inflates false positives.** Run twenty independent tests at p < 0.05 and you expect one spurious "discovery" by chance alone. Correct for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni divides the threshold by the number of tests) or you will find patterns that are not there. ##### Naive Bayes: probability as a classifier Bayes' theorem applied directly gives a working classifier. It is "naive" because it assumes features are independent given the class — usually false, and it works surprisingly well anyway. ```python from collections import defaultdict import math, re class NaiveBayesSpam: def __init__(self, alpha: float = 1.0): self.alpha = alpha # Laplace smoothing self.word_counts = {"spam": defaultdict(int), "ham": defaultdict(int)} self.class_counts = {"spam": 0, "ham": 0} self.vocab: set[str] = set() @staticmethod def tokenize(text: str) -> list[str]: return re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text.lower()) def fit(self, messages: list[str], labels: list[str]) -> None: for msg, label in zip(messages, labels): self.class_counts[label] += 1 for word in self.tokenize(msg): self.word_counts[label][word] += 1 self.vocab.add(word) def _log_prob(self, words: list[str], label: str) -> float: total_docs = sum(self.class_counts.values()) # Work in LOG space: multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0 score = math.log(self.class_counts[label] / total_docs) # prior total_words = sum(self.word_counts[label].values()) denom = total_words + self.alpha * len(self.vocab) for word in words: if word in self.vocab: count = self.word_counts[label][word] score += math.log((count + self.alpha) / denom) # likelihood return score def predict(self, message: str) -> str: words = self.tokenize(message) return max(("spam", "ham"), key=lambda c: self._log_prob(words, c)) clf = NaiveBayesSpam() clf.fit( ["win free money now", "claim your prize winner", "cheap meds free trial", "meeting at three tomorrow", "can you review the report", "lunch next week"], ["spam", "spam", "spam", "ham", "ham", "ham"], ) print(clf.predict("free prize claim now")) # spam print(clf.predict("review the meeting notes")) # ham ``` Two implementation details carry real weight. **Laplace smoothing** (`alpha`) prevents a single unseen word from zeroing the entire probability. And **working in log space** turns multiplication into addition, avoiding numerical underflow when multiplying hundreds of small probabilities — a technique you will see throughout machine learning. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Prior belief
P of A] --> B[Observe evidence B] B --> C[Likelihood
P of B given A] C --> D["Bayes: posterior ∝
likelihood × prior"] D --> E[Updated belief
P of A given B] E -.becomes the new prior.-> A ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Ignoring the base rate**, as in the medical-test problem — the core of imbalanced-class confusion. - **Reading a p-value as "probability the hypothesis is true."** - **Reporting significance without effect size.** - **Multiple comparisons** without correction, manufacturing false discoveries. - **Assuming correlation implies causation**, or missing nonlinear relationships because the coefficient was near zero. - **Using the mean when outliers are present** instead of the median. - **Forgetting `ddof=1`** for sample standard deviation. - **Multiplying probabilities directly** instead of summing logs, causing underflow. - **Assuming normality** without plotting a histogram or Q-Q plot. - **Accuracy as the sole metric** on imbalanced data. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: use NumPy and SciPy to **generate samples from normal and binomial distributions, compute summary statistics, and visualize histograms**. Verify the 68-95-99.7 rule empirically on your normal sample, and watch the binomial approach normality as `n` increases — that convergence is the Central Limit Theorem happening in front of you. The mini project is a **Naive Bayes spam classifier from scratch**. Use the implementation above as a reference, then extend it: test it on a real SMS spam dataset, and report precision and recall separately rather than accuracy. On an imbalanced dataset, that split is where the base-rate lesson becomes concrete. For the assignment, use **Bayes' theorem on a medical test** to compute the probability that a positive result is a true positive, **and explain the intuition**. The explanation matters more than the arithmetic — describe the 100,000-people walkthrough, because the counting version is what actually convinces people. Then connect it back: state what this implies for a fraud model deployed where fraud is 0.1% of transactions. That connection is the reason this topic is on the roadmap. ##### Key takeaways - Base rates dominate: a highly accurate test for a rare condition still produces mostly false positives, which is exactly the imbalanced-class problem in ML. - Bayes' theorem converts measurable `P(evidence|hypothesis)` into the `P(hypothesis|evidence)` you actually want, and evidence accumulates across updates. - The normal distribution and the 68-95-99.7 rule give you fast intuition about whether a value is unusual; the mean is outlier-sensitive while the median is not. - Correlation misses nonlinear relationships and never implies causation — plot the data and consider confounders before concluding anything. - P-values do not measure the probability a hypothesis is true; always report effect size, and correct when testing many hypotheses.
